name: Mira's sunlight, vitamin D and calcium

parameters.label: Hours outdoors in daylight each week
parameters.explain: Skin makes vitamin D when sunlight's UVB falls on it. In summer, 5–30 minutes on bare skin a couple of times a week is usually enough.

parameters.label: Season
parameters.explain: Between October and early March, sunlight in northern countries is too weak for skin to make enough vitamin D.

parameters.label: Glasses of milk a day
parameters.explain: Tests the 'just drink more milk' idea. Each cup has about 300 mg of calcium — but how much gets in depends on vitamin D.

parameters.label: Skin uncovered outdoors
parameters.explain: Covered skin makes no vitamin D — clothes, sunscreen and even window glass block the UVB.

parameters.label: Milk has added vitamin D
parameters.explain: Almost all US milk has about 120 IU of vitamin D added per cup — helpful, but three glasses is still less than a teen needs.

overlay.caption: sunlight on skin → vitamin D → gut takes in calcium → bones

explain.summary: Bones are built from calcium, which Mira gets from milk. But her gut can only take much calcium in when there is enough vitamin D, and most vitamin D is made by skin in sunlight. In winter, with a coat on and almost no daylight, her skin makes very little — so much of her milk's calcium passes straight through, even though she drinks plenty.
rules: Her skin makes vitamin D in proportion to hours outdoors, how much skin is uncovered and how strong the season's sunlight is.
Winter sunlight makes almost none; summer sunlight makes a lot.
Her daily vitamin D is sun plus food (fortified milk adds about 120 IU a cup); a teen needs about 600 IU.
With enough vitamin D the gut absorbs about 30% of calcium; with too little, much less.
Calcium absorbed = calcium eaten × the share absorbed.

source.fact: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, one of the main building blocks of bone. Teens aged 14–18 need 15 mcg (600 IU) a day; a cup of fortified milk has about 3 mcg (120 IU), and almost all US milk is fortified. Clothing, sunscreen, clouds and window glass reduce how much vitamin D skin makes.
About 5–30 minutes of sun on exposed skin, especially between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., daily or at least twice a week, usually leads to enough vitamin D; season and time of day change this.
Between October and early March people in the UK don't make enough vitamin D from sunlight; from late March to September most people can make all they need.
A cup of milk has about 276–299 mg of calcium; about 30% of calcium from dairy is absorbed, and vitamin D is required for that absorption.
Teens aged 14–18 need 1,300 mg of calcium a day.

choice.what: Vitamin D made per outdoor hour: about 20 (winter), 150 (spring/autumn) and 400 (summer) IU a day for each weekly hour of face-and-hands-sized skin
choice.why: Picked so a little summer sun covers the daily need, as the sources say, while winter sun makes almost none.

choice.what: Calcium absorption goes from 10% (very low vitamin D) up to 30% (enough)
choice.why: Sources give about 30% with enough vitamin D and say less is absorbed without it; 10% is our estimate for the low end.

choice.what: Other food adds 250 mg of calcium and 40 IU of vitamin D a day
choice.why: A rough allowance for the rest of her diet.

choice.what: 'Getting enough' means absorbing about 370–390 mg of calcium a day
choice.why: That is roughly 30% of the 1,300 mg teens are advised to eat.

illustrative: Mira is fictional; her 3 hours outside, 3 glasses of milk and winter coat are made up for the story.
The location of 'northern country' winter sunlight is general; real amounts depend on latitude, cloud and skin colour.

citations.title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Consumers
citations.supports: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium; ages 14–18 need 15 mcg (600 IU) a day; fortified milk has about 3 mcg (120 IU) per cup and almost all US milk is fortified; clothing, sunscreen, clouds, dark skin and window glass reduce skin production.

citations.title: Vitamin D — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
citations.supports: Season, time of day, cloud cover, smog, skin melanin and sunscreen affect vitamin D synthesis; about 5–30 minutes of sun (10 a.m.–4 p.m.) daily or twice a week usually suffices; vitamin D promotes calcium absorption in the gut.

citations.title: Vitamin D
citations.supports: From late March to September most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight; between October and early March we do not make enough from sunlight; vitamin D helps regulate calcium.

citations.title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
citations.supports: One cup of nonfat milk has 299 mg of calcium (whole milk 276 mg); about 30% of calcium from dairy and fortified foods is absorbed; vitamin D is required for active calcium absorption in the gut.

citations.title: Calcium — Fact Sheet for Consumers
citations.supports: Recommended calcium for ages 14–18 is 1,300 mg a day; milk, yogurt and cheese are the main food sources; vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
